text: Learning when to stop and request human intervention.
Turn off the main water shutoff valve.
Turn off the main electrical breaker.
Operate a household fire extinguisher (pull pin, aim, squeeze, sweep).
Unlock and open a window specifically for emergency egress.
Plug cables into rear I/O ports by feel or from tight visual angles (e.g., distinguishing DisplayPort from HDMI by touch/shape).
Provide a stable, locked-joint physical brace for a person attempting to stand up or sit down.

Guide a visually impaired person through a cluttered room (acting as a sighted guide).Caring for people (must-have). Most entries are about objects and rooms. People mostly show up as obstacles or as someone to hand things to.

Wake someone up; help someone sit, stand, or steady themselves; offer an arm on stairs; help with buttons, zips, and shoes; fetch and clean glasses and hearing aids; push or fold a wheelchair or walker.

Accessibility beyond mobility: describe layout and obstacles for low-vision residents, read mail and labels aloud, flash lights for the doorbell and alarms for deaf residents, keep furniture in consistent positions, dementia-friendly routines (labels, door checks).

section: Emergency response (must-have). Detection and alerting are covered well, but active response is thin.
text: Detect: a person who has fallen or is unresponsive, calls for help or choking sounds, glass-break or forced-entry sounds, gas smell, a car running in a closed garage, a child near stairs, a pool, or a stove.

Primitives: communication is thin (you have Report, Alert, and Ask for clarification). Add Speak, Listen, Announce, Explain, Confirm, Refuse, Undo, Hand off to a human, Remember, Forget. Physical verbs also missing: Cut/Slice, Peel, Crack, Tear, Hammer, Drill, Climb, Kneel/Crouch, Balance, Throw/Catch, Point/Gesture, Spray, Brush.

Situational variations. Apartments and condos (elevators, shared laundry, HOA rules), regional standards (metric vs. imperial, front vs. top-load, induction vs. gas, shoes-off homes), languages, accents, and speech differences, residents with disabilities or dementia, residents' emotional states, and robot-side degradation (dirty camera, low battery, network down, a failing arm).
“Make this place look nice.” There may be no single correct state; it has to reason about symmetry, spacing, aesthetics, furniture placement, and household preferences.
“Put everything back where it belongs.” It may never have seen the objects or their normal locations before.
“Hide this somewhere the dog can’t reach it.” Requires reasoning about the pet’s reach, jumping ability, room access, and object safety.
“Make some room.” Requires rearranging objects without making the environment worse.
“Set this room up for a party.” Number of guests, seating, food locations, walking paths, decorations, trash locations, and breakable objects all matter.
“Set this room back to normal.” Requires remembering the previous room state.
“Clean whatever needs cleaning.” Requires inspection, prioritization, and deciding when something is clean enough.
“Fit everything into the trunk.” A 3D packing problem involving fragile, heavy, accessible, and awkwardly shaped objects.
“Unload the car and put everything away.” It has to classify items and route them to different locations.
“Bring in the groceries, but take the frozen stuff first.” Requires prioritizing temperature-sensitive items.
“Find something I can stand this on.” Requires assessing stability and load.
“Carry this without tipping it.” Requires estimating center of mass and liquid movement.
“Carry all of these in one trip if you can.” Requires deciding how objects can be stacked, held, bagged, or transported together.
“Move this without scratching the floor.” Requires modifying the plan based on surface and object material.
“Clean under there without moving everything.” Requires selecting tools and alternate approaches.
“Clean behind the couch.” The robot must determine whether it can reach, move the couch, use an attachment, or request help.
“Clean the spots people usually miss.” Requires knowledge of common cleaning failures.
“Something is leaking. Find it.” Requires tracing evidence to a source.
“There’s a weird noise somewhere.” Requires localization, appliance knowledge, and anomaly detection.
“Something fell upstairs. Check what happened.” Requires investigating an uncertain event.
“Make sure nothing looks wrong.” General anomaly detection across an open world.
“Check whether anything changed since I left.” Requires storing and comparing previous environmental states.
“Find what’s missing.” Requires knowing the expected inventory.
“Find my keys.” Requires systematic search and understanding likely human placement habits.
“Find the thing I was using earlier.” Requires tracking recent human-object interactions.
“Find the remote; I think someone moved it.” Requires probabilistic search.
“Look somewhere I wouldn’t normally put it.” Requires modeling abnormal human behavior.
“Find something my kid hid.” Requires adversarial search through plausible hiding locations.
“Find where the dog took my sock.” Requires reasoning about pet behavior.
“Put it over there.” Requires understanding gestures and shared spatial reference.
“Straighten this.” Requires determining the intended reference line.
“Make sure nobody trips over anything.” Requires hazard identification from a human perspective.
“Keep the cat out while you clean this room.” Requires simultaneous task execution and dynamic agent management.
“Help me carry this.” Requires synchronized cooperative manipulation with a human.
“Move when I move.” Requires adaptive cooperative control.
“Fix the wobbly table.” Requires diagnosing whether the issue is loose hardware, uneven floor, damaged leg, etc.
“Make this shelf level.” Requires sensing, adjustment, and iterative verification.
“Do it without moving the sleeping baby.” Requires low-noise, low-vibration planning.
“Clean quietly.” Requires changing tools and motion profile.
“Do it without waking anyone up.” Requires reasoning about doors, floors, lights, vacuum noise, dishes, etc.
“Clean while people are still using the kitchen.” Requires dynamically working around moving humans and active tasks.
“Do this whenever you get a chance.” Requires scheduling around other priorities.
“Figure out what changed and update everything accordingly.” A general reconfiguration problem.
“Figure it out.” Possibly the ultimate generalization benchmark: inspect state, infer intent, construct a plan, act, detect failure, recover, and know when to ask for help.

“Catch this falling object.” Requires dynamic reflexive control, predicting the trajectory of an object in freefall, and deciding whether it is safe to catch (e.g., catching a falling cup vs. letting a falling knife hit the floor).
“Carry this stack of plates quietly.” Requires modifying a standard walking gait to act as an active suspension system, minimizing vertical vibration.
“Read the room.” If humans are having a tense argument, or someone is crying, the robot must infer that it should cancel its noisy vacuuming task and leave quietly.
“Stop.” / “Not like that.” / “Undo that.” Requires halting safely, working out what to revert, and restoring the prior state.
“Is that pan still hot?” / “Is this safe to stand on?” Requires inferring temperature or stability before touching.
“Something fell behind the fridge.” Requires retrieving it without moving the appliance.
